title: Chunky garter triangle shawl
subtitle: A quick top-down triangle in chunky wool, on 6 mm needles.
excerpt: A top-down triangular shawl in chunky wool on 6 mm needles, worked flat in plain garter stitch to a wingspan of 120 cm. At roughly 14 stitches per 10 cm the rows grow fast and the whole shawl knits up in a weekend. About 250 g of chunky wool.
sourceNotes: Top-down triangular construction is a widely published folk technique. The garter-stitch triangle in chunky weight is a modern adaptation of a century-old structure. No single original source.

knitting.gaugeText: 14 sts × 28 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 6 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan 120 cm. Centre-back depth 55 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small strip of garter stitch worked on a few stitches, then rotated so live stitches can be picked up from all three edges, giving a neat triangular start at the centre back neck.

content.text: A top-down triangular shawl in chunky wool on 6 mm needles, worked flat in garter stitch to a wingspan of 120 cm and a centre-back depth of 55 cm.

The chunky weight grows fast at 14 stitches per 10 cm: the full shawl is roughly 165 rows of knitting, which most knitters finish in two evenings. The construction is top-down, starting at three stitches at the centre back neck and increasing four stitches on every right-side row. There is nothing to track except where the increases sit. Budget about 250 g (about 330 m / 360 yards) of chunky wool. It drapes well across the shoulders for cold-weather wear and sits flat over a coat.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 250 g (330 m / 360 yards) of chunky-weight yarn
items.substitutions: Any chunky-weight wool or wool blend. A high wool content blocks better and gives a softer drape than acrylic chunky.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 6 mm (UK 4 / US 10) straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.qty: 1, for weaving in ends — choose one with an eye large enough for the chunky yarn

content.text: Gauge

14 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 6 mm needles, blocked. Swatch a 15 cm square, block it, and measure the centre 10 cm once dry. At chunky weight even a small gauge difference has a noticeable effect on the finished dimensions: if your blocked swatch reads 15 stitches per 10 cm instead of 14, the finished wingspan will be about 112 cm rather than 120 cm at the same row count. Move up to 6.5 mm needles if your gauge is tight.
Stitches used

items.name: yo
items.qty: yarn over: bring yarn to front, then over needle before next knit stitch. Adds one stitch.

content.text: Pattern
Garter tab cast-on
Start with a
garter tab
to create a clean centre-back neck point.
Using waste yarn, cast on 3 stitches using a knitted-on cast-on.
Knit 6 rows with the waste yarn.
Switch to main yarn. Knit the 3 sts on the needle (RS).
Without turning, pick up and knit 3 sts along the left long edge of the tab (1 per ridge).
Pick up and knit 3 sts along the cast-on edge (remove waste yarn as you go). 9 sts total.
Knit 1 WS row. Place markers: marker A after st 1, marker B (spine) after st 5, marker C after st 8.
Increase section
Work the two-row repeat until wingspan reaches 120 cm.
RS (increase row): k1, yo, SM, k to 1 st before marker B, yo, k1, SM, k1, yo, SM, k to last st, yo, k1. (4 sts increased)
WS: k all sts.
After 78 RS rows you will have 9 + (4 × 78) = 321 stitches and a wingspan of approximately 120 cm at gauge.
Stitch count check-ins
After 25 RS rows: 9 + 100 = 109 stitches. Check the marker positions are still centred: each half-wing should have the same stitch count.
After 50 RS rows: 9 + 200 = 209 stitches. At this stage the wingspan is about 77 cm and the centre-back depth is about 36 cm. A good point to try the shawl across the shoulders.
Bind off

Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off: *k1, yo towards the front of work, k1, pass both the yo and the first k st over the second k st; repeat from *. A standard bind-off will hold the wingspan back when the shawl is pinned to 120 cm, so it springs in when the pins are removed.
Common faults

Uneven wings: one side has more stitches than the other. Usually caused by working one increase twice on the same side, or skipping one increase on the other. Count each wing section separately every 15 RS rows and fix with a partial row if needed.

Garter ridges not lining up across the spine: the spine stitch was accidentally moved by a stitch. The two centre markers define a single stitch; the stitch on either side of them is the last stitch of each wing, not a separate centre st.

Chunky yarn splitting at the yo: hold the right needle tip firmly against the yarn as you bring it forward for the yarn over, rather than dragging the needle through. A yo on chunky yarn can split if the needle tip catches the plies.
Blocking

Soak in cool water for 10 minutes. Press out water in towels without wringing. Pin out on a blocking mat to the stated dimensions. Chunky wool blocks to shape well and holds the wingspan when pinned. Allow 24 to 36 hours to dry fully before removing the pins, since chunky yarn dries slower than fine yarn.
Care
Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble dry. Chunky wool felts if agitated in hot water.
What to try next

The same construction in DK wool on 4 mm needles gives a lighter-weight shawl with a longer wingspan for the same yardage. Alternatively, add a two-stitch garter border along each wing edge and a simple eyeleted stripe every 20 rows to introduce a first lace element.
